stem: A software team wants to configure a shared Model Context Protocol (MCP) server across their repository so all teammates can access it, while ensuring API secrets are not committed to version control. Where should this configuration be placed?

options.text: In the global ~/.claude.json file with static credentials encrypted by the local operating system keychain.
In the project-level .mcp.json file using environment variable expansion for the required authentication tokens.
In the repository's root CLAUDE.md file, embedding the server command and token inside a fenced json code block that Claude Code parses on startup.
In the local scope entry for this project — the projects["<repo-path>"].mcpServers block inside ~/.claude.json — using the same environment variable expansion for the token.

explanation: Shared MCP servers should be declared in the project-level .mcp.json file, which is committed to version control so team members share the server definition. Sensitive credentials should be referenced via environment variable expansion (such as ${API_KEY}) so secrets remain out of the repository.

distractorNotes.a: The global ~/.claude.json file is user-specific and is not shared across teammates via version control.
distractorNotes.c: CLAUDE.md supplies natural-language project context and is not parsed as a structured MCP server declaration, and hardcoding the token there still commits the secret to version control.
distractorNotes.d: Local scope also lives in ~/.claude.json, keyed under the user's own project-path entry rather than the repository; it stays private to that machine and is never committed through the project's version control, so teammates would not receive the server definition.

sourceNote: Configure MCP servers in project-scoped .mcp.json with environment variable expansion

stem: A logistics support agent has two tools: track_shipment (description: 'Returns shipment information.') and get_carrier_account (description: 'Returns carrier information.'). Each takes a single string parameter named id. Logs show that when users paste a tracking number and ask where their parcel is, Claude often calls get_carrier_account. What should the team change first?

options.text: Add input_examples to both tools showing typical id values, tracking numbers for one and account numbers for the other, while keeping the one-line descriptions.
Detect tracking-number patterns in application code and set tool_choice to {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'track_shipment'} on those requests.
Rewrite each description to say what the tool returns, when to use it and when not to, which id formats it accepts, and how it differs from the other.
Rename the tools with a shared service prefix, such as carrier_track_shipment and carrier_get_account, so the names are namespaced by provider.

explanation: The tool-definition guidance calls detailed descriptions "by far the most important factor in tool performance": a description should explain what the tool does, when it should and shouldn't be used, what each parameter means, and its caveats. Two one-line descriptions over identically named id parameters give Claude nothing that separates a tracking number from an account number, so the descriptions are the first thing to fix.

distractorNotes.a: input_examples are recommended for complex, nested or format-sensitive inputs, but the guidance is to prioritize clear descriptions; example id values alone still do not tell Claude when each tool applies and when it does not.
distractorNotes.b: Forcing a tool from application-side pattern matching replaces Claude's selection instead of fixing what it selects from, and any request the pattern misses still reaches the same two ambiguous descriptions.
distractorNotes.d: Service prefixes make selection unambiguous when tools span multiple services or resources; both tools here belong to the same carrier service, so a shared prefix adds nothing that tells them apart.

sourceNote: Best practices for tool definitions - extremely detailed descriptions are the most important factor in tool selection

stem: An agent has two tools with high functional overlap: analyze_content and analyze_document. Claude frequently chooses the wrong tool or calls both redundantly. How should the architect refactor the tool definitions?

options.text: Set model temperature to 0.0 so the model deterministically selects between the two overlapping tools.
Add explicit priority hints to each tool description telling Claude to prefer analyze_document over analyze_content whenever both could apply.
Add a negative constraint in the system prompt explicitly instructing Claude never to invoke analyze_document when analyze_content could apply.
Rename the tools to reflect distinct operational domains (e.g. extract_web_text vs parse_pdf_document) with non-overlapping descriptions.

explanation: Overlapping tool names and vague descriptions create semantic confusion for the model. Renaming tools to clearly indicate their specific operational scope (e.g. distinguishing web scraping from PDF parsing) and eliminating overlapping responsibilities in their descriptions gives Claude unambiguous criteria for tool selection.

distractorNotes.a: Zero temperature does not resolve semantic ambiguity between overlapping tools; it simply makes the arbitrary misselection deterministic.
distractorNotes.b: Priority hints do not remove the underlying semantic overlap; Claude still cannot tell which tool fits a given input, so it keeps misselecting or calling both.
distractorNotes.c: Negative prompt instructions do not resolve semantic ambiguity between tools with identical capability descriptions; the model still struggles to determine which tool genuinely applies to a given input.

sourceNote: Eliminating functional overlap in tool naming and descriptions to prevent misselection

stem: An engineering team exposes a single monolithic manage_data tool that accepts an 'action' parameter covering twelve CRUD operations and thirty optional fields. In production, Claude frequently confuses parameter combinations, passing update arguments during read operations and hallucinating missing fields. How should the architect refactor this interface?

options.text: Split the monolithic tool into focused, purpose-specific tools, each with strict JSON schemas declaring only their relevant parameters.
Retain the monolithic tool but define conditional oneOf schema blocks to enforce valid parameter combinations for each action at runtime.
Add comprehensive few-shot examples to the system prompt illustrating valid parameter sets for each action while keeping the single tool schema.
Implement a client-side wrapper that intercepts failed tool executions and feeds backend validation error traces back to Claude for re-prompting.

explanation: The exam guide lists splitting generic tools into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts as a tool-interface design skill. Replacing the twelve-action manage_data tool with focused tools (e.g. `create_record`, `read_record`, `archive_record`), each declaring only its own parameters, removes the irrelevant fields Claude was mixing across operations.

distractorNotes.b: The Claude API doesn't accept oneOf at the schema root; Claude Code flattens such a schema and describes each branch's required parameters in the tool description instead of enforcing them, so the parameter-combination confusion remains.
distractorNotes.c: Few-shot prompting increases prompt token consumption and latency without resolving the underlying schema ambiguity of a 30-parameter monolithic tool.
distractorNotes.d: Client-side error retry loops are reactive, add latency, and waste tokens attempting to recover from failures that proper tool decomposition prevents deterministically.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 2.1 - splitting generic tools into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts

stem: An agent has well-designed tools for customer queries, but the system prompt contains the sentence: 'Always use search to find user details.' As a result, Claude calls the general web search tool instead of the specialized lookup_customer tool. What explains this failure?

options.text: Because the API places the user system prompt after the tool definitions, Claude reads the directive as lower-priority context and falls back to whichever tool appears last in the tools array.
Keyword-sensitive phrasing in the system prompt created an unintended strong association that overrides clear tool descriptions.
The web_search tool advertises a broader capability surface, and Claude's selection logic prefers the more general tool whenever two tools could plausibly satisfy a request.

Tool descriptions alone determine selection, with no influence from system prompt wording, so a sufficiently detailed lookup_customer description should already have overridden the generic 'search' phrasing regardless of what the system prompt says.

explanation: The exam guide notes that keyword-sensitive instructions in a system prompt can create unintended tool associations that override well-written tool descriptions. 'Always use search to find user details' ties user lookups to the web search tool by keyword, so the fix is to review and reword the system prompt rather than the tool definitions.

distractorNotes.a: The constructed prompt does place tool definitions before the user system prompt, but that ordering does not demote the system prompt or create a positional fallback; here the system prompt directive is exactly what biased the choice.
distractorNotes.c: Claude does not automatically favor the 'broader' tool; with clear descriptions it selects the specialized one. The regression here comes from the generic 'search' directive in the system prompt, not from capability breadth.
distractorNotes.d: Tool descriptions are weighed together with the system prompt and the query, not in isolation; a well-written lookup_customer description does not insulate it from being overridden by a competing, tool-name-matching directive elsewhere in the prompt — which is exactly the failure in this scenario.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 2.1 - keyword-sensitive system prompt instructions can create unintended tool associations

stem: An MCP server tool encounters a backend database connection timeout. How should the tool return this error to the agent according to Model Context Protocol standards?

options.text: Return a protocol-level JSON-RPC error response with code -32000 (Server error) to indicate that the tool execution failed.
Return an empty JSON object with HTTP status 200 to simulate a successful query that returned zero rows from the backend store.
Return a tool result with isError: true containing structured metadata with error category, retryable flag, and diagnostic context.
Return a normal tool execution result with isError: false and format the timeout exception message as plain markdown in the text content.

explanation: A database timeout is a transient tool failure, which the MCP isError flag pattern communicates back to the agent as a tool result with `isError: true`. Including structured error metadata, such as an error category (transient/validation/permission), an isRetryable flag and a human-readable description, lets the agent make an appropriate recovery decision instead of guessing.

distractorNotes.a: The MCP specification reserves protocol errors (standard JSON-RPC errors) for issues with the request itself, such as an unknown tool, malformed requests or server errors, which models are less likely to fix. A backend API failure such as a database timeout is a tool execution error, reported in the tool result with isError: true.
distractorNotes.b: Masking failures as successful empty responses misleads the agent into believing data does not exist.
distractorNotes.d: Returning error messages with isError: false misinforms the client framework that the tool invocation succeeded, preventing automated error handling and recovery workflows.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 2.2 - the MCP isError flag pattern with structured error metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable)

stem: An agent calls process_refund, but the customer's purchase exceeds the 30-day return policy window. How should the tool response be structured to prevent the agent from repeatedly retrying the failed call?

options.text: Return a generic 'Request Failed' message and allow the agent to retry with exponential backoff until the timeout window expires.
Return isError: true with isRetryable: true and a generic message, letting the agent's exponential backoff eventually give up after its maximum retry count.
Return a tool execution result with isError: false and an empty payload, prompting the agent in the system prompt to infer policy rejection.
Return isError: true with isRetryable: false, specifying the business policy constraint and human-readable explanation.

explanation: An expired return window is a business rule violation, not a transient failure, so retrying cannot succeed. The exam guide describes returning structured metadata that marks the error as non-retryable together with a customer-friendly explanation, which prevents wasted retry attempts and lets the agent explain the policy to the customer.

distractorNotes.a: A uniform 'Request Failed' response hides whether the failure is transient or permanent, so the agent cannot make an appropriate recovery decision and may keep retrying.
distractorNotes.b: Marking a permanent policy violation as retryable makes the agent waste tokens on retries that can never succeed before finally failing without a clear explanation for the customer.
distractorNotes.c: Returning isError: false for a failed business rule violation misinforms the agent that the operation succeeded and forces unreliable probabilistic inference from missing fields.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 2.2 - non-retryable flags and customer-friendly explanations for business rule violations

stem: In a multi-agent system, a web search subagent experiences a transient network timeout on an external provider. How should error recovery be partitioned between the subagent and coordinator?

options.text: The subagent attempts local retries with exponential backoff; if unrecoverable, it propagates structured failure context and partial results to the coordinator.
The subagent forwards every transient error straight to the coordinator without any local retry, so that all backoff and retry policy lives centrally in one place.
The subagent falls back immediately to an unverified local cache, returning stale search results without error metadata to maintain latency.
The coordinator wraps the subagent in its own exponential-backoff loop and re-invokes the entire subagent on any failure, discarding partial results between attempts.

explanation: Transient failures such as a brief network timeout are handled by local recovery inside the subagent. Only errors that cannot be resolved locally are propagated to the coordinator, together with partial results and what was attempted, so the coordinator can decide the higher-level recovery (e.g. trying an alternative source or proceeding with partial results).

distractorNotes.b: Centralizing all retries forces a cross-agent round trip for glitches the subagent could resolve itself, adding latency; transient, self-contained failures should be retried locally before escalating.
distractorNotes.c: Silently returning stale unverified cached data masks operational failures from the coordinator and risks propagating inaccurate or obsolete facts into synthesis.
distractorNotes.d: Re-invoking the whole subagent throws away partial progress and structured failure context and treats every failure as retryable; recovery should begin locally and propagate structured context upward.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 2.2 - local error recovery in subagents, propagating unresolved errors with partial results

stem: An agent queries a customer directory tool using search_users(email='unknown@example.com'). The underlying database query executes successfully but matches zero rows. According to tool design best practices, how should the tool response be structured?

options.text: Return a tool result with isError: true and an HTTP 404 status code indicating that the requested customer record was not found.
Return a successful tool result (isError: false) containing an empty list or 'No records found' status.
Return isError: false paired with an HTTP-style 204 No Content response and no body, since the query executed successfully with no rows.
Return a protocol-level JSON-RPC error with code -32602 (Invalid params) indicating that the provided email parameter is unresolvable.

explanation: A search that runs successfully and matches nothing is a valid empty result, not an access failure. The exam guide separates the two because only access failures need retry decisions; returning `isError: false` with an empty list or clear status lets Claude conclude the user does not exist instead of treating the result as a failure to retry.

distractorNotes.a: A search that successfully finds zero matches is a valid empty result, not an access failure; setting isError: true pushes Claude into retry or debugging decisions for a query that already succeeded.
distractorNotes.c: MCP tool results are JSON-RPC responses with structured content blocks, not HTTP responses; there is no analogous '204 No Content' status, and an empty body still leaves the model without a content block stating that the search matched zero rows.
distractorNotes.d: The parameters passed were syntactically and semantically valid; returning an invalid-params protocol error misrepresents a successful database query as a client formatting defect.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 2.2 - distinguishing access failures from valid empty results

stem: An engineering team binds twenty-five distinct enterprise tools to a single general-purpose agent. During evaluation, tool selection accuracy drops from 94% to 68%. What architectural factor explains this degradation?

options.text: The additional tools introduce overlapping parameter schemas, and JSON Schema validation conflicts between similarly named fields cause the API to reject roughly a third of the tool calls.
Each added tool schema proportionally shrinks the context left for the user's request, so the model loses the conversational detail it needs to choose correctly.
Over-provisioning tools increases cognitive decision complexity and semantic overlap, impairing model selection reliability.
The larger combined schema size triggers Claude Code's context-management auto-compaction mid-session, which discards earlier tool-call examples and drives the accuracy drop.

explanation: Giving an agent too many tools degrades selection reliability by increasing decision complexity and the semantic overlap among similar operations; the cited guidance is that fewer tools reduce selection ambiguity, so restricting each agent to the tools its role needs restores accuracy.

distractorNotes.a: The API validates each tool call against that tool's own schema independently; overlapping field names across different tools do not cause rejections. The degradation is selection difficulty, not schema validation failures.
distractorNotes.b: Twenty-five tool schemas do not exhaust the context window; accuracy falls because of decision complexity and semantic overlap among similar tools, not because conversational context was crowded out.
distractorNotes.d: Auto-compaction discards earlier conversation turns under context pressure over a long session; it is a multi-turn state-management mechanism, not a cause of degraded tool-selection accuracy on individual calls, and the drop comes from selection ambiguity among overlapping tools, not to context truncation.

sourceNote: Cognitive complexity and selection degradation from tool over-provisioning

stem: In a research system, the report synthesis subagent frequently attempts to run broad web searches when it encounters missing context, exceeding its latency budget and duplicating the search agent's work. What configuration enforces proper boundaries?

options.text: Add a warning in the user prompt telling the synthesis agent that web searching is strictly discouraged during report generation.
Lower the synthesis agent's temperature to 0 so it deterministically stops issuing search calls whenever it detects that context is missing.
Place a routing classifier in front of the synthesis agent that inspects each turn and returns any search request to the coordinator instead of executing it.
Scope the synthesis agent's allowedTools to only formatting and drafting tools, removing external search tools entirely.

explanation: The principle of least privilege in agent architecture dictates that each subagent should only have access to the tools necessary for its dedicated role. Removing web search tools from the synthesis agent's `allowedTools` configuration deterministically prevents it from deviating into information retrieval.

distractorNotes.a: Prompt warnings are probabilistic and do not prevent tool calling when the model feels information is missing.
distractorNotes.b: Temperature controls sampling randomness, not tool availability; a low-temperature model still calls a search tool it has access to when it judges that context is missing.
distractorNotes.c: An external classifier adds latency and complexity and only reactively blocks calls after the model has decided to make them; removing the tools from allowedTools prevents the behavior deterministically at the source.

sourceNote: Restricting subagent tool sets via allowedTools to enforce functional separation of concerns

stem: In a support system, a reply-drafting subagent often needs an order's current status while writing a response. Each check now goes back to the coordinator, which invokes an investigation subagent that holds the warehouse, carrier and payment tools. Most checks are a single order's status; a few need records correlated across all three systems. What should the architect change?

options.text: Give the drafting subagent the investigation subagent's warehouse, carrier and payment tools, so it can settle each check itself without returning to the coordinator.
Let the drafting subagent spawn the investigation subagent directly as a nested subagent for each check, removing the coordinator hop from the path.
Give the drafting subagent a narrowly scoped, read-only get_order_status tool for single-order checks, and keep routing cross-system cases through the coordinator.
Have the drafting subagent collect its status checks and return them to the coordinator as one batch after finishing the draft, cutting the trips to one.

explanation: The exam guide's tool-distribution guidance is to give each agent only the tools its role needs, plus limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs, while complex cases are still routed through the coordinator. A single-order status tool covers the frequent simple check without a round trip, and the rare cross-system investigation keeps its existing path.

distractorNotes.a: Handing the drafting subagent the investigator's full toolset over-provisions it; agents given tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them, and the rare cross-system case no longer goes through the coordinator.
distractorNotes.b: Nesting the investigation subagent removes one hop but still runs a full multi-system investigation for a simple status lookup, and moves orchestration out of the coordinator.
distractorNotes.d: The draft depends on the statuses it checks, so deferring every check until the draft is finished forces a rewrite once the results return instead of removing the delay.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 2.3 - scoped cross-role tools for high-frequency needs, complex cases routed through the coordinator

stem: An extraction workflow requires that the agent must invoke the extract_metadata tool on the first turn before any enrichment tools can be considered. How should the API request be configured?

options.text: Add input_examples to the extract_metadata tool definition demonstrating the desired call sequence, since Claude treats those examples as an enforceable execution order across turns.
Set tool_choice: {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'extract_metadata'} to force the model to invoke that specific tool.
Include a strict execution directive in the system prompt instructing Claude to always execute extract_metadata before calling any other tool.
Set tool_choice: 'any' so the model is forced to call a tool, which guarantees extract_metadata runs before any other tool on the first turn.

explanation: The Messages API supports forced tool selection via `tool_choice: {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'tool_name'}`. This forces Claude to generate a call to the specified tool on that turn, guaranteeing that `extract_metadata` executes before subsequent turns allow other tools.

distractorNotes.a: input_examples are schema-valid example arguments that help Claude format a single tool's inputs correctly; they carry no cross-tool sequencing semantics and do not constrain which tool is called on which turn — only tool_choice: {'type': 'tool', ...} does that.
distractorNotes.c: System prompt directives are probabilistic; while they guide model reasoning, they do not guarantee deterministic tool selection or execution order like the tool_choice parameter does.
distractorNotes.d: tool_choice: 'any' forces the model to call some tool but lets it pick which one; it does not pin the first call to extract_metadata specifically.

sourceNote: Forcing specific tool invocation using tool_choice parameter

stem: A system provides three specialized extraction tools (extract_invoice, extract_receipt, extract_contract). The input document type is unknown in advance, but the application requires that Claude MUST execute one of the tools rather than returning conversational text. Which setting guarantees this?

options.text: tool_choice: {'type': 'none'}, which disables tool calling entirely and forces the model to respond with plain conversational text instead of a structured tool call.
tool_choice: {'type': 'auto'}, which lets Claude decide for each document whether to invoke an extraction tool or respond with plain conversational text instead.
tool_choice: {'type': 'any'}, which forces Claude to invoke one of the provided tools while allowing it to select which extraction schema fits the document.
tool_choice: {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'extract_invoice'}, which guarantees a tool call but forces invoice extraction even on receipt or contract documents.

explanation: Setting `tool_choice: {'type': 'any'}` forces Claude to invoke at least one tool from the available tools list, but allows the model to select which specific tool best matches the input document. This guarantees structured tool invocation while preserving dynamic tool selection.

distractorNotes.a: tool_choice: {'type': 'none'} disables tool use entirely, forcing text-only responses.
distractorNotes.b: tool_choice: {'type': 'auto'} lets Claude choose whether to execute a tool or respond conversationally, failing the requirement to guarantee tool execution.
distractorNotes.d: Forcing a specific tool name guarantees execution but eliminates dynamic tool selection, inappropriately forcing extract_invoice on receipts and contracts.

sourceNote: Guaranteeing tool calling over conversational text using tool_choice: any

stem: A developer wants to experiment with a personal SQLite MCP server without sharing it with team members in git, while keeping existing project-level MCP tools active. How should this be configured?

options.text: Add the SQLite server to .mcp.json and run git update-index --assume-unchanged on the repository to avoid committing local changes.
Hardcode the SQLite path in the global CLAUDE.md file, instructing the model to invoke it via natural language descriptions.
Define the SQLite server in a project-root .mcp.local.json file, which Claude Code automatically loads while keeping it excluded from git.
Configure the SQLite server in ~/.claude.json, allowing Claude Code to load it alongside project-level servers from .mcp.json.

explanation: Claude Code supports a multi-tier MCP configuration hierarchy. Project-scoped servers committed to version control live in `.mcp.json`, while user-scoped personal servers reside in `~/.claude.json`. Claude Code loads servers from all configured scopes together, so the personal server is available alongside the project's .mcp.json servers.

distractorNotes.a: Git index manipulation is brittle and easily overwritten by team merges, branch checkouts, or clean clones.
distractorNotes.b: CLAUDE.md provides natural language instructions, not structured JSON MCP server configurations.
distractorNotes.c: Claude Code does not recognize .mcp.local.json; local private configurations must be placed in ~/.claude.json to remain separate from the shared project .mcp.json.

sourceNote: Configuring personal MCP servers in ~/.claude.json alongside project .mcp.json

stem: An MCP server provides access to an issue tracker. To understand existing components, the agent currently executes 4-6 exploratory search tool calls per session. How can the MCP server reduce this latency and token overhead?

options.text: Expose the component hierarchy and schema as an MCP Resource (URI), enabling the client to attach it directly without exploratory tool calls.
Embed the complete component taxonomy directly inside the description field of the issue creation tool schema so it loads on every turn.
Implement an MCP Prompt template that executes a dynamic client-side SQL query against the issue database on each user turn.
Configure the MCP server to cache prior exploratory search results in local server memory across independent agent sessions.

explanation: MCP Resources provide a standardized mechanism for servers to expose read-only data, schemas, or catalog hierarchies via URIs. Exposing catalog data as resources allows the client/agent to read the structured taxonomy directly or attach it as context, eliminating repetitive exploratory tool invocations.

distractorNotes.b: Embedding large taxonomies in tool descriptions inflates prompt token consumption on every turn regardless of whether the tool is invoked.
distractorNotes.c: Prompts are user-controlled, interactive prompt templates requiring explicit invocation; they do not provide standardized application-attached context data.
distractorNotes.d: Server-side caching may speed up backend database queries but does not eliminate the client-agent round trips or token costs of the 4-6 exploratory tool invocations.

sourceNote: Using MCP Resources to expose structured catalogs and schemas without exploratory tool calls

stem: A team adds an MCP server providing a Jira integration tool, but Claude Code consistently uses Grep and Bash to find issue details in local git logs instead of calling the Jira tool. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Jira tool is withheld from Claude until the user references it with an @ mention, because Claude Code exposes MCP capabilities only when they are attached explicitly, as it does with MCP resources.
The Jira MCP tool description is vague and fails to convey its capabilities and output fields, causing Claude to prefer familiar built-in tools.
The Jira MCP tool schema defines complex nested parameters without default values, causing Claude Code to bypass the tool to avoid validation errors.
MCP tools connecting over stdio transports are restricted to read-only commands whenever local repository files match query keywords.

explanation: When an MCP tool has an impoverished or generic description (e.g. 'Jira operations'), the model cannot discern its utility and falls back on built-in tools like Grep and Bash whose capabilities and outputs are well understood. Writing rich, descriptive tool documentation solves this preference bias.

distractorNotes.a: @ mentions attach MCP resources; MCP tools are discovered by Claude itself (via tool search by default) without any user reference. The cause here is the impoverished description.
distractorNotes.c: Claude selects tools based on description relevance and capability matching before evaluating parameter schemas; schema complexity does not cause silent fallback to Grep and Bash.
distractorNotes.d: Claude Code does not restrict stdio MCP tools based on query keyword matches against local repository files.

sourceNote: Crafting rich MCP tool descriptions to prevent fallback to generic built-in tools

stem: While modifying a configuration file, Claude Code's Edit tool repeatedly fails with an error stating that the target text chunk is not unique. What is the standard tool-based fallback mechanism?

options.text: Invoke the Bash tool to execute a sed replacement command targeting the line numbers reported in the Edit error message.
Repeatedly invoke Edit with allowMultiple: true to overwrite all matching occurrences across the file without anchoring lines.
Use Read to inspect the full file with surrounding lines, then use Write to overwrite the entire file with the accurate modifications.
Execute the Glob tool to locate duplicate occurrences, then invoke Edit with force: true to bypass the uniqueness constraint.

explanation: The Edit tool requires a unique string match to ensure targeted replacements. When the target content occurs multiple times and cannot be uniquely anchored, the exam guide's fallback is to use Read to obtain the full file context, apply the modifications in memory, and use Write to save the updated file safely.

distractorNotes.a: Invoking sed via Bash is fragile, platform-dependent, and bypasses Claude Code's safe file editing lifecycle; the exam guide's fallback uses Read and Write.
distractorNotes.b: The Edit parameter is replace_all, not allowMultiple, and replacing every occurrence changes all matches rather than the single intended one.
distractorNotes.d: The Edit tool does not support a force: true flag to override uniqueness checks.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 2.5 - Read + Write as the fallback when Edit cannot find unique anchor text

stem: An enterprise architecture team evaluates the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification to integrate internal repositories and services into Claude. During review, the team contrasts how different MCP primitives operate and who controls their execution. Which TWO statements accurately describe the operational models and control planes of MCP primitives? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Prompts provide autonomous background event triggers that automatically initiate agent tool executions whenever underlying resource URIs change state on the remote MCP server.
Resources provide application-controlled, read-only data access identified by fixed URIs or dynamic URI templates, allowing the host to supply context without model execution.
Resources provide model-controlled execution endpoints that allow Claude to directly invoke state-changing database write operations and arbitrary operational shell scripts.
Tools provide model-controlled executable interfaces with typed JSON Schema definitions, allowing the model to autonomously invoke operations that query or modify external systems.
Tools provide static, parameter-free text snippets that users must manually select from an interactive client menu before an LLM can inspect their underlying schema definitions.

explanation: According to the MCP server concepts documentation, MCP primitives have distinct control and operational models: Resources are application-controlled, read-only data sources addressed by fixed URIs or URI templates that the client retrieves to attach context to the model turn without model execution. Tools are model-controlled executable interfaces defined by JSON Schema that the LLM autonomously discovers and calls to perform queries or state-changing actions. Prompts are user-controlled, parameterized templates requiring explicit user invocation.

distractorNotes.a: Prompts are user-controlled templates requiring explicit invocation (such as via slash commands or UI palettes); they do not act as background event listeners or automatic triggers.
distractorNotes.c: Resources are passive, read-only data endpoints controlled by the application; active execution and state modifications must be implemented as Tools.
distractorNotes.e: Tools are schema-defined, parameterized interfaces discovered and invoked autonomously by the model, not static user-selected menu snippets (which describes Prompts).

sourceNote: Core Server Features table and operational control models for Tools, Resources, and Prompts

stem: A platform team standardizes Model Context Protocol (MCP) configuration across engineering projects using Claude Code. Developers configure servers across local scopes (~/.claude.json), project scopes (.mcp.json), and user scopes (~/.claude.json). Which TWO statements accurately describe Claude Code's scope precedence and configuration isolation rules? (Select TWO.)

options.text: If a server name is defined in both local and project scopes, Claude Code uses the local definition exclusively, without merging configuration fields across scopes.
Claude Code performs a deep merge across overlapping scopes, applying user-scoped headers and environment variables on top of project-level command declarations.
Project-scoped servers in .mcp.json are committed to version control for team sharing, whereas local- and user-scoped configurations remain private to the developer.
User-scoped servers defined in ~/.claude.json take precedence over project-scoped .mcp.json definitions to ensure personal settings override team defaults.

Project-scoped .mcp.json servers connect without an approval prompt when the repository's own committed .claude/settings.json sets enableAllProjectMcpServers, even in a folder the developer has not yet trusted.

explanation: Claude Code enforces a strict scope precedence hierarchy: Local scope > Project scope > User scope (followed by plugins and connectors). When the same server name appears across multiple scopes, Claude Code connects using the definition from the highest-precedence scope in its entirety without merging fields or environment variables. In addition, project-scoped servers defined in .mcp.json are tracked in git for team collaboration, whereas local- and user-scoped servers in ~/.claude.json remain strictly private to the individual developer.

distractorNotes.b: Claude Code selects the entire server definition from the highest-precedence source; configurations and environment variables are never deep-merged across scopes.
distractorNotes.d: The precedence hierarchy is local > project > user, so project-scoped configurations override user-scoped definitions, not the reverse.
distractorNotes.e: A cloned repository can't approve its own servers: enableAllProjectMcpServers committed to the project's .claude/settings.json is ignored in an untrusted folder, and the server stays at Pending approval.

sourceNote: Scope hierarchy, precedence, and field isolation across local, project, and user scopes

stem: An engineer tasks Claude Code with diagnosing an unhandled application event: InvoicePaymentFailed within a repository containing hundreds of nested packages. To trace the event to its dispatch point and handler logic without consuming unnecessary context window tokens, which built-in tool invocation strategy should Claude Code use?

options.text: Run Glob with the pattern **/InvoicePaymentFailed* to locate files associated with the event name, then invoke Read on the returned file paths to inspect their internal contents.
Execute Read across all files in the project directory simultaneously to construct a comprehensive in-memory symbol graph before searching for specific identifier strings.
Use Grep to search file contents for the string InvoicePaymentFailed to locate entry points, then use Read selectively on matching files to trace the execution flow.
Execute a recursive find and grep command via the Bash tool across the repository tree, streaming all matching output directly into the conversational context.

explanation: Claude Code is designed to build codebase understanding incrementally. Using Grep allows Claude to search file contents across the repository for specific string literals, function identifiers, or event dispatchers without reading unnecessary files. Once entry points are identified, Claude selectively uses Read on those specific files to trace imports and execution paths, minimizing context window usage and avoiding early compaction.

distractorNotes.a: Glob performs pattern matching on file paths and file names, not file contents. Unless a file happens to be named after the event string, Glob will not locate where InvoicePaymentFailed is defined or handled.
distractorNotes.b: Reading numerous files upfront fills the context window with irrelevant code, burning tokens and triggering auto-compaction that degrades model performance.
distractorNotes.d: The flaw is volume rather than the shell: streaming every match as raw stdout into the conversation spends far more context than a targeted Grep call followed by selective Read of the files it names, which is the incremental pattern the stem asks for.

sourceNote: Grep tool behavior for searching file contents and Read for inspecting code

stem: An organization connects six Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers providing over fifty tools for database management, ticket tracking, and cloud deployment to Claude Code. Despite the large number of integrated tools, the developer observes that sessions start with minimal context token consumption before any tool is called. What architectural mechanism explains this behavior?

options.text: Claude Code imposes a fixed per-server tool limit, loading schemas for the first few endpoints and omitting the remainder from the prompt.
Claude Code loads each server's tool list from a discovery cache saved in a previous session, so tool schemas never enter the context window.
Claude Code embeds all fifty schemas into a local vector index on startup, retrieving matching tool schemas via similarity search on each turn.
Claude Code enables tool search by default, deferring full tool schemas and loading only tool names and server instructions until needed.

explanation: Claude Code implements MCP tool search by default to keep context consumption low when connecting multiple MCP servers. Instead of loading every tool's complete JSON schema into the prompt upfront, Claude Code defers tool schemas and loads only tool names and server instructions at session start. When Claude determines that an external tool is required, it discovers and retrieves the full parameter definitions on demand.

distractorNotes.a: Claude Code does not impose a fixed per-server or per-session tool cap; tool search allows scaling across many servers without arbitrarily truncating tool catalogs.
distractorNotes.b: The discovery cache does exist, but it stores a server's tool list so Claude Code can defer connecting until Claude first calls one of its tools; it governs connection timing rather than schema deferral, is off by default, and cached tools are still available from the first message.
distractorNotes.c: Claude Code does not embed schemas into a local vector index or perform cosine similarity retrieval; it uses native MCP tool search (tool_reference blocks), where Claude inspects deferred tool names and server instructions and requests schemas on demand.

sourceNote: Scale with MCP tool search by deferring tool schemas until needed
